title: Chain-of-Thought Is Not Sufficient for Explainability
claim: Current explanations can be unfaithful, rooted in hidden mechanisms and widespread misuse, so a set of verification directions is needed.
layout: 3 columns, left-to-right: problem, insights, roadmap; example with arrows at left
description: A three-column overview figure with column headers Problem, Insights and Roadmap. At left, a rounded box holds a question about whether the product of the two smallest primes exceeds their sum. Three arrows lead to three quoted chain-of-thought answers. Each answer has red highlights marking an error: a wrong sum, a generic 'yes' to any prime question, and a wrong shortcut. Icons and labels below name the failure types: restoration errors, bias-driven answers and unfaithful shortcuts. In the centre, one box shows a neural network whose internal computation picks a different option from the written steps. Below it, an arXiv analysis box shows 1,000 papers, a magnifier and a pie chart with a red 21.7% slice. At right, a tall rounded container stacks six future research directions in rounded boxes. Red is used for errors and key numbers, and everything else is black and white.
caption: Overview of our paper: Unfaithful Chain-of-Thought behaviours (left), their mechanistic and cognitive underpinnings (centre), and proposed research for enhancing Chain-of-Thought faithfulness (right).
abstract: Chain‑of‑thought (CoT) allows language models to verbalise multi‑step rationales before producing their final answer. While this technique often boosts task performance and offers an impression of transparency into the model's reasoning, this position paper argues that rationales generated by current CoT techniques can be misleading, and are not on their own sufficient evidence of faithful explanation. We analyse faithfulness as whether CoTs are not only human-interpretable but also reflect the model’s underlying reasoning well enough to support responsible use. By synthesising evidence from prior work, we systematically show that verbalised chains are frequently unfaithful, diverging from the critical hidden computations that drive a model's predictions. As CoT is increasingly relied upon in application domains, including high-stakes ones such as medicine, law, and autonomous systems, we further argue that this unfaithfulness is not taken seriously enough in these settings: our analysis of 1,000 recent CoT-centric papers finds that approximately 21.7\% explicitly treat CoT as a load-bearing interpretability technique, building pipelines or safety arguments that would not hold if CoT is unfaithful to the model's actual reasoning. They include papers in high-stakes domains that heavily hinge on such interpretability claims. Building on prior work, we make three proposals: (i) avoid treating CoT as being sufficient for interpretability without additional verification, (ii) adopt rigorous methods that assess faithfulness for downstream decision-making, and (iii) report such assessments alongside any interpretability claims based on CoT, while continuing to use CoT for its communicative and monitoring benefits.
